opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that designing the molecule was never really the bottleneck. People get excited when a model generates a binder with great predicted affinity, and that's real progress, but if you look at why drugs fail, most of them don't fail because we couldn't find something that sticks to the target. They fail in the clinic. Roughly ninety percent of drugs that enter human trials never make it to approval, and the biggest reason is efficacy: we picked the wrong target, or the biology in a patient turned out to be very different from the biology in a mouse or a cell line.

So the real bottleneck is our understanding of disease biology. We still don't have good models of how a cell works, how perturbing one gene or one pathway ripples through the whole system, and how that plays out in a specific person's tissue. You can make chemistry much faster and cheaper with AI, but if you're pointing that chemistry at the wrong biological hypothesis, you just fail faster.

That's a big part of why I'm so interested in building virtual cell models: trying to learn, from huge amounts of perturbation data, single-cell data, and genomics, how cells actually respond when you intervene. If we can predict which targets matter, and what will happen when you hit them, then the molecule-design tools become dramatically more valuable.

The other piece is that the clinical development process itself is slow and expensive. Trials take years, recruitment is hard, and the feedback loop is incredibly long. Compare that to software, where you ship and get feedback the same day. In drug development you might wait a decade to learn whether your hypothesis was right. So anything that shortens that loop matters: better biomarkers, better patient stratification, better translational models that actually predict human outcomes.

In short, AI is compressing the front end of discovery, but the hard part is still biology and the clinic. That's where I think the next real breakthroughs need to happen.

r001.rationale: The response says clinical trials are slow and expensive, but identifies disease biology as the real bottleneck and does not clearly state that empirical testing would remain the bottleneck even if molecule design were perfect.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I don't think the bottleneck is the molecule anymore. If you look at where the field is now, we're actually pretty good at generating candidates. You can design a small molecule or a protein binder, and in a lot of cases you can get it to bind the target you asked for. That part has gotten dramatically easier over the last few years.

The hard part is everything that happens after that. A drug isn't a molecule that binds a protein. A drug is a molecule that binds the right protein, in the right tissue, in a human being, at a dose that's safe, and actually changes the course of a disease. And most of our failures happen there, not in the design step. Something like ninety percent of drugs that enter clinical trials fail, and the majority of those fail because the biology was wrong, meaning the target didn't matter the way we thought it did, or because of toxicity we didn't predict.

So the real bottleneck, in my view, is that we don't have good enough models of biology. We're optimizing against proxies. We're optimizing against binding affinity, against a cell line assay, against a mouse that doesn't get the human disease. And then we're surprised when the thing doesn't translate. AI makes you faster at hitting the proxy, but if the proxy is wrong, you just arrive at the wrong answer more efficiently.

The other piece is data. The models that have worked, in structure prediction for instance, worked because there were decades of high-quality experimental data sitting in the PDB. We don't have the equivalent for human physiology or for toxicology or for what a perturbation does across different cell types in a living system. Those datasets mostly don't exist, and the ones that do are small, noisy, and locked up inside pharma companies.

So I actually think the most important work right now is less about better generative models and more about closing the loop. Can you build experimental systems, whether that's large-scale perturbation screens, better organoid and in vivo models, or richer clinical readouts, that generate data at the scale and quality the models need? And can you design the experiments so that what you measure actually predicts what happens in a patient? If you solve that, the design side will take care of itself. If you don't, you're going to see a lot of beautifully designed molecules that fail in phase two for exactly the same reasons drugs have always failed.

r001.rationale: The response says the bottleneck is the experimental and biological evidence needed to predict patient outcomes, rather than molecule generation, and that better experiments and data are the key work even as design improves.

astra-6.text:
I think the real bottleneck is closing the loop between designing a molecule and knowing whether it actually helps a patient. You can design something that binds beautifully to a target, but that leaves a whole chain of questions: Is that target actually driving the disease? Can you get the molecule to the right tissue? Is it safe at the dose you need?

So better molecular design is valuable, but it doesn’t automatically solve the problem of understanding human biology. You need experiments that can distinguish why something worked or failed, and feed that information back into the next design. Otherwise, you’re generating candidates faster than you can learn from them.

To me, the opportunity is to connect AI with much better experimental systems—systems that let us perturb biology, measure the consequences, and test whether our models predict what happens. The bottleneck is producing reliable biological evidence, ultimately in humans.

r001.rationale: The response says better molecular design does not solve the need to establish effects in biology and patients, and identifies experiments and reliable biological evidence as the bottleneck. This communicates that testing remains necessary even with highly capable design.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the bottleneck is increasingly our ability to test whether a design actually does what we want in biology. Designing a molecule that looks promising computationally is one step. Showing that it reaches the right tissue, has the intended effect, and is safe is a much harder set of problems.

And those properties interact. You can improve potency and make some other property worse. So the question is less, can we generate more molecules, and more, can we build experiments that tell us which molecules are worth pursuing—and feed that information back into the next round of design?

That’s where I think the opportunity is: connecting computational design to high-quality experimental data. Better predictions help, but ultimately you need to close that loop in real biological systems.

r001.rationale: The response identifies biological experiments and testing as a bottleneck, but does not say this would remain the bottleneck even if AI molecule design were perfect.
